activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Lily sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma put a pencil in her hand. "Can I write my name?" Lily asked. "Yes, let's try," said Grandma.

Lily held the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard on the paper. The letters came out big and wobbly. One letter looked like a stick. Her L came out wrong. Lily made a sad face. "It won't do what I want," she said.

Grandma sat close by. "Watch my hand," she said. Grandma pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. Lily looked and looked. Then she tried it. Pinch, pinch, rest. She wrote an L. Then an I. Then more letters. L, I, L, Y. "Look, Grandma, look!" said Lily. Grandma smiled big. On the paper, the name stood clear and neat, letter after letter, all the way across the empty page.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Henri was awake early. Today was his first day of school. He put on his red shoes. He packed a triangle sandwich in his bag. "A triangle has three sides," he said.

At the classroom door, Henri stopped. His tummy felt funny. It fluttered like a small bird. He held Mama's hand tight.

"My tummy feels fluttery," Henri said.

"I felt that way on my first day too," Mama said. "Feeling nervous is okay."

Henri looked at the door. He took one step. Then another step. Inside, a boy was chasing a ball across the rug. The boy smiled at Henri. Henri smiled back.

"My tummy is quiet now," Henri said. He let go of Mama's hand and ran to chase the ball too.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Josephine went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to find something pretty to look at. First she saw the big grill by the benches. It had a small fire inside. It was hot. Grandma held her hand. "We stay far from the fire," said Grandma. The fire made the grill go hiss and pop. So standing far away was the good thing to do.

Next Josephine saw a picnic table. On the table was a little bag. The bag was open. Inside were round red things and round yellow things. They looked like candy. Were they candy? Josephine wanted to touch them. She did not touch them. She kept her hands right at her sides.

"Grandma, come and see," she called. Grandma came and looked. "Those are not candy," said Grandma. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Grandma picked up the bag and put it in her pocket. She said Josephine was very kind to come get her.

A boy ran up. He beg, beg, begged to see the pretty round things. "No," said Grandma. "Not for touching." The boy and Josephine ran to the swings instead. Josephine pumped her legs. Up, up, up she went. "Look at me!" she called. Grandma waved and waved.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the bookshop with Mama. A friendly lady worked there. Her name was Miss Ada.

Brooklyn found a rug with letters on it. "Look, Mama! Letters!" she said. She sang her letter song. "A, B, C, D," she sang. She sang all the way to P. Then she stopped.

"Is P the last letter?" she asked.

Miss Ada smiled. "Keep going," she said. "There are more letters after P."

Brooklyn sang on. "Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Z."

"Z is the last letter," said Miss Ada. "The alphabet starts with A and ends with Z."

Brooklyn looked at the rug. She pointed at the A. "A says ah," she said. Then she pointed at the B. "B says buh."

"Now try my name," said Miss Ada. "A-D-A."

"Ah, duh, ah. Ada!" said Brooklyn. The letters made a name! She clapped her hands.

"Can I spell my name too?" she asked.

"You can," said Mama.

Brooklyn looked for the B. She found it near the A, at the very start of the alphabet.

"There you are, B!" she said. "You are first."

She traced the letter with her finger, round and round.

"Time for dinner soon," said Mama. "But first, one more song?"

Brooklyn sang from A all the way to Z. Then she waved at the rug.

"Bye, letters," she said. "See you after Z... I mean, after A!"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Sara was at the farm with Grandpa. She dug little holes in the brown soil. She put tomato seeds in one row. She put carrot seeds in another row. Then she patted the soil down and watched the seeds sink out of sight.

The next day, tiny green leaves came up. Sara forgot which row was which. "Where are my tomatoes?" she asked. Grandpa handed her some sticks and paper. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," he said. Sara drew a red tomato on one paper and a long orange carrot on the other. She stuck them in the soil, one for each row.

"Now I know, now I know!" said Sara. Grandpa found a pretty stone and a small old bone to edge her garden path. Each morning Sara watered the rows. Each morning she read her labels. Then one green ball grew on the tomato plant. Sara held it in her two hands and smiled. "Look, Grandpa! The tomato label was right!"

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Victor was at school. It was snack time. Ms. Beth had a big jug of apple juice. She poured juice into little cups.

Ben pushed to the front. "Give me juice!" he said. Ms. Beth shook her head. "Try again," she said. Ben frowned. Then he said, "Juice, please." Ms. Beth smiled. "Of course!" She poured him a big cup.

Victor watched all this. He was very thirsty. He wanted juice too. He waited in line. His tummy felt jumpy. Then it was his turn. "Juice, please," said Victor. Ms. Beth poured his cup all the way up. "Thank you," said Victor. "You are welcome," said Ms. Beth.

Later, Victor bumped into Ben's elbow. Juice spilled on the table. "Sorry," said Victor. Ms. Beth helped wipe it up. "It was an accident," she said. Afterward Victor felt warm inside, not sleepy, just happy. On the way to the rug he heard Ben say, "Blocks, please." The teacher said yes. Victor smiled and sat down with his empty cup.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Harrison had a big pot on the balcony. "We can grow lettuce," said Dad. Harrison put three seeds in the soil. He patted the soil until it was smooth. Dad wrote the letter L on a stick. "L for lettuce," said Harrison, and he pointed at the stick.

Every day Harrison looked. One sprout. Then two. Then three little green leaves. He counted them. "One, two, three," said Harrison.

One day the sun was hot. The lettuce hung down low. "It looks sad," said Harrison. He felt worried. Dad gave him the watering can. "Give them a drink," said Dad. Harrison tipped the can. Drip, drip, drip, all over the leaves.

The next morning, Harrison ran to the balcony. The lettuce stood up tall. "One, two, three," he counted. All three plants were up. "They wanted water," said Harrison. Dad smiled. "More water tomorrow," said Harrison, and he filled the little can.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Joshua was playing with his blocks. Then he heard a noise. Thump, thump, thump. It came from the hall. Joshua felt scared. His tummy felt tight. His dog, Biscuit, ran to the door. Biscuit began to bark.

Joshua wanted to know what made the noise. But he felt too scared to look. He remembered what Grandpa said. "When you are scared, tell a grown-up you trust." So Joshua called out, "Daddy!"

Daddy came fast. He held Joshua's hand. They walked to the hall together. Daddy turned on the light. "Let's listen," he said. Thump, thump, thump. It came from the big tree by the window. A branch was tapping the glass.

Daddy opened the window a little bit. He moved the branch away. The tapping stopped. Joshua felt happy now. His tummy felt calm. "The tree made that noise," Joshua said. "The wind pushed the branch," said Daddy. Joshua smiled big. He felt so excited. "Biscuit, we found it!" he said. Biscuit wagged his tail. Joshua gave Daddy a cool high five. Then he ran back to his blocks. He was not scared anymore.

story:
Claire ran into Grandma's kitchen. She wanted to make soup for her teddy bear. Grandma gave her a big pot and a wooden spoon.

Claire found some pretend food. There were red apples and yellow pears. They looked so real. Claire put one in her mouth.

"Spit it out, sweet pea," said Grandma. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat."

Claire spat it out. Then she stirred her pot. She put in pretend apples and pretend pears. She held the spoon up to teddy's mouth. "Slurp, slurp," said Claire. Teddy was full!

Outside, a bird began to sing its last song of the morning. Claire carried her pot to the window. A little red leaf flew past the glass and landed in her pot.

"A leaf in my soup!" said Claire. "That is the best surprise ever." Grandma laughed and clapped her hands.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Isaac climbed into the car. He held his snack. But Bunny was gone! "Where did Bunny go?" he cried. Mom looked under the seat. It was too dark to see. "We can't see in there," said Mom. Isaac felt like crying.

"Wait!" said Mom. She opened the glove box. She took out a flashlight. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots," said Mom. She clicked it on. Mom shined the light under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore! Isaac leaned over and looked.

"I see a tail!" he shouted. "Bunny is there!" Isaac reached down. His arm was too short. Mom unbuckled him. Then he reached again. His fingers touched soft fur. He pulled and pulled. Out came Bunny! "Bunny!" Isaac hugged her tight.

"Now we can go," said Mom. She drove past the kitchen shop on the corner. Isaac waved at it. The car went round and round the bend. "That bend makes me dizzy!" Isaac laughed. Bunny sat on his lap all the way home. "No more dark spots for you," said Isaac. Mom smiled and kept driving.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Natalie sat on the playroom floor. Her tummy felt hungry for a game. Mama held up a big blue bag.

"This is the feely bag," said Mama. "Put your hand in. Don't peek!"

Natalie put her hand inside the bag. She felt something round. It was smooth. It had a little bounce.

"A ball!" she said. "A red ball!"

Natalie pulled it out. She looked at it. It was not red. It was yellow!

"Oh," said Natalie. "I could feel it was a ball. But my fingers did not tell me the color."

Mama smiled. "Want to try again?"

Natalie reached into the bag. She felt something soft and squishy. A sock! But what color? She had to look. She pulled it out fast. Green!

Then Mama hid a red car in the bag. Natalie felt the little wheels. She felt the smooth top. But she shut her eyes and squeezed it. Still no color came to her fingers.

"Is it red?" she asked.

"Look and see," said Mama.

Natalie opened her eyes. Yes! The little car was red.

"One more," said Natalie. She filled the bag with her blue blocks herself. Then she closed her eyes tight and reached in.

Mama laughed. "You can feel the blocks, Natalie. But only your eyes can find the blue."

Natalie peeked with one eye. There it was. Blue!

"My eyes are so good," said Natalie. She gave the bag a big hug.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Margot sat at the little table. The tablet lay in front of her. The screen was dark and still. She wanted to draw a cat on it.

She tapped the dark screen with her finger. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. Still nothing. "Why won't it wake up?" she asked.

Teacher Ben came over. He was a grown-up, so he knew about tablets. "Press the button," he said. He pointed to the small button on the side. Margot pressed it. The screen lit up. It was bright and full of colors. Her tap had not worked, but her press did.

She pressed the drawing app and drew a big cat. It had long whiskers and a winter scarf, because outside the window snow was falling. When she was done, she pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, just where it belonged.

"I did it," Margot said, and she clapped her hands.

story:
Wesley was a small boy who loved the forest. He found a flat stump under a big tree. He put three pinecones and two leaves on top. "This is my shop," he said.

A squirrel came near and sat still. Wesley waited. The squirrel did not pick anything. Then his friend Mia came down the path. "I am the shopkeeper," said Wesley. "You can be the shopper." Mia picked one leaf. She paid him with a small stone. Wesley put the stone in his pocket.

"Now I can be the shopper," said Wesley. "You be the shopkeeper." Mia stood by the stump. Wesley walked around the tree first. Then he came back. He picked one pinecone and paid with the stone. He put the pinecone in his bag to carry home. "Good shop," said Mia. The squirrel watched from the branch above.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Gabriella went to Miss Penny's music room. Miss Penny had a small drum. She wanted Gabriella to clap the steady beat. Gabriella wanted to sing "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" all by herself. But first she had to clap.

Gabriella clapped. Her claps went fast, faster, fastest. "Too fast," said Miss Penny. "Let's try marching." Miss Penny marched around the room. Gabriella marched too. Her footsteps went one, two, one, two. They stayed even and they kept going. "Like this!" said Gabriella. She clapped along with her marching feet. Clap, clap, clap. The claps were even now. The claps kept going too.

"Now sing," said Miss Penny. Gabriella sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, yes sir, yes sir." Miss Penny played the drum. Gabriella clapped the steady beat and sang every word. Miss Penny clapped too. "I did it!" said Gabriella. Miss Penny smiled and gave her a hug.

story:
Hazel went to the library with Dad. She wanted the big red book about a chicken. The shelves were tall. She could not reach it.

A boy named Sam stood by the shelf. He had a book in his hands. Hazel reached up high. Her hand bumped Sam's book. The book fell down with a thump.

"Sorry," said Hazel. She picked up the book. She gave it back to Sam. Sam smiled. "Thank you," he said.

Hazel wanted the red chicken book still. She asked the librarian. "Please, can you help me?" The librarian reached up high. She took down the red book. "Here you go," she said.

"Thank you," said Hazel. She sat on the soft rug. Dad sat next to her. Hazel opened the book. The chicken had fresh yellow feathers. Sam came and sat too. They read together, page by page, until the story swung its happy ending.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Logan stood in the library with his mom. He wanted a book about trucks. He could not take it home. The lady at the desk said, "You need a library card."

Logan reached up on his toes. "Can I have one?" he asked. The lady shook her head. "A grown-up helps a child sign up," she said. So Mom sat down at the desk. She wrote on the paper. Logan watched and held his book against his knee.

Then the lady made a little card. It was blue and shiny. It had Logan's own name on it! She put it in his hand. Logan gave the book to her. She beeped it. Now the book was his to take home. "Thank you," Logan whispered. He squeezed Mom's hand and skipped to the door.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emily was at Grandma's house. She wanted a cookie. She saw a big jar on the shelf. There were little marks on the jar. "What are those marks, Grandma?" Emily asked. Grandma said, "Those are words. Words tell us things."

Grandma lifted Emily up so she could see. Emily pointed at the jar. "What do the words say?" she asked. "They say Cookie Jar," said Grandma. Emily looked and looked. Words on a jar! Words were telling her what was inside!

Then Emily saw a box on the table. It had words too. "What does the box say?" she asked. "It says Crackers," said Grandma. Emily clapped her hands. Words on boxes! Words everywhere!

There was a little card on the door. It had words on it. "What does the card say?" asked Emily. "It says Welcome," said Grandma. Emily smiled. Words on signs! Words told her things all day.

Grandma brought a book to the soft chair. She sat Emily on her lap. "Books have words too," said Grandma. She opened the front of the book. She turned one page, then the next. She read from the front to the back.

Emily leaned on Grandma's warm neck. Her neck did not hurt at all. It was comfy and soft. Grandma read about a little green frog. The frog sat on a slimy rock by the pond.

"More words," said Emily. "Read the front to the back again!" Grandma turned to the first page. She began to read. Emily listened, happy and warm.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Dylan wanted to go to the park. He could see the swings from the window. The park was across the street. He called, "Grandma, park!"

Grandma came with her shoes on. She took the bread out of the oven first. The pan was hot. She used a big glove so her hand would not get hurt. Dylan stayed back from the oven. He saw steam go up, up, up.

Outside, the sun was warm. The street was in front of them. Dylan saw a red truck go by. He held Grandma's hand. They looked left. They looked right. They walked across the street together, hand in hand.

At the park, Dylan found crunchy leaves. He stepped on them. Crack, crack! Grandma sat on the bench. A little girl dropped her ball. Dylan picked it up and gave it back. She smiled big.

When they got home, Dylan was sleepy. He got into his bed with his bear. "We held hands," he said to the bear. Then he closed his eyes.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Stella wanted to play at school. Ben and Mia were in the corner. They rocked a doll and stirred a tiny pot.

Stella stood and watched. She did not know how to join. She scratched her head. "What do I say?" she asked herself.

Then she had an idea. "Let's pretend I'm the doctor!" she said. Ben looked up right away. "Yes! Our baby bear is sick," he said. Mia patted a chair. "Sit at the table, Doctor Stella."

Stella listened to the bear's tummy. "He needs a hug and a nap," she said. The bear got a blanket. He closed his eyes.

Then Mia said, "Let's pretend we're pirates!" The table became a big boat. Stella was so lucky. One little sentence had started three games.

"Roar," said Ben. "A sea monster!" The boat rocked and rocked, and Stella held on tight.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Zoey was in the garage with Grandpa. He had a little guitar made of wood. "You can play it," Grandpa said.

Zoey picked a string. The sound was funny. It went boing, not a nice note. She picked another string. Boing again. "It sounds wrong," she said.

Grandpa sat down next to her. "The strings need tuning," he said. "Then the notes sound right." He turned the little pegs at the top. Zoey watched. He turned one peg a tiny bit.

Zoey picked the string again. Now it made a sweet note. Not boing. A real note! "I want to try," she said. Grandpa helped her turn a peg. Very slow. Very small.

Zoey picked the string. The note sounded mean and wobbly. Too far! Grandpa smiled. "Turn it back a little," he said. Zoey turned it back. She picked the string. Sweet note.

"Again!" said Zoey. She picked every string, one by one. Grandpa tapped his foot to her song.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Sienna put on her new backpack. It sat on her back. It was very heavy. She walked to the school playground. Her legs felt slow.

"Oof," said Sienna. She could not run. The bag pulled her back.

A boy named Tom ran up. "That's a backpack," he said. "It rides on your back."

Sienna sat on the bench. She opened the bag. She looked in. Three teddy bears! Two books! One drum!

"Too many toys," said Sienna. She took out the teddy bears. She took out the drum. The bag got thin and light now.

Sienna stood up. The air felt good on her face. She ran to the slide. Tom ran with her. They laughed all the way.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Adam sat at the little table at school. Miss Kim put out ten fresh leaves for counting. Adam touched each leaf one by one. "One, two, three," he said. His friend Mia counted too. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Miss Kim sang the counting song, and everyone sang the last word together. "Ten!"

Adam wanted to write ten on his paper. He wrote a big 1. Then he stopped. The other numbers had one shape each. Ten looked different. "Why does ten need two numbers?" he asked. Miss Kim smiled and knelt down beside him. "Ten is a 1 and then a 0," she said.

Adam wrote the 1. Then he wrote the 0 right after it. Mia looked over at his paper. "That is ten!" she said. Adam picked up a leaf and gave it to Mia. She took a tiny bite of her apple and grinned. Then Adam counted all ten leaves again, tapping each one. Ten leaves, ten numbers, one happy boy.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Georgia sat on Grandpa's big striped chair. Everyone was watching the game. The room was loud. People clapped and cheered.

"Who is winning?" Georgia asked. She clapped her hands too, just like the big people.

"Watch the numbers," said Grandpa. He pointed at the screen. "The red team has two. The blue team has two. It is a tie."

"A tie," said Georgia. She said it again. "A tie."

The game went on. Georgia waited. She waited some more. Her cousin Sam gave her a cracker. She munched it slowly. The night was coming outside the window.

Then the blue team kicked the ball. It went in the net. Everyone jumped up. "One more for blue!" they shouted. The score was not the same now. Red had two. Blue had three.

"The tie is gone," said Grandpa. "Blue is winning now."

Georgia looked at the screen. She pointed at the numbers. "Not a tie," she said. "Blue has more."

The game ended. Blue had three. Red had three again. The big people all sat down.

"It's a tie!" Grandpa laughed. "The same score again."

Georgia stood on the rug and clapped. "A tie," she said. "A tie for everyone!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Rehmat was playing in the backyard. She wanted to make a cold drink for her doll, Dolly. It was a hot day, and Dolly sat in the sun.

Papa brought out a bowl of ice cubes. Rehmat picked one up with her fingers. She touched it and pulled her hand back fast. "Cold, cold!" she said. She dropped the ice cube right into Dolly's cup. She touched it again with one finger. It was still cold.

Rehmat looked at the shiny ice with her eyes. She heard it go plink in the cup with her ears. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled like water. She licked it with her tongue. It tasted like water too. "Your drink is ready," she said. She put Dolly under a tree, out of the sun. Then she touched her own cold, wet cup and smiled. "Papa, Dolly calls this her mountain of ice," she said. Papa laughed and helped her add one more piece.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Colton went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his little blue car. It was his favorite toy.

The car slipped out of his hand. It went down, down, down. "Where did it go?" said Colton. "Where did it go?"

Colton looked by the apples. No car. He looked by the bread. The bread was in a thick plastic bag. No car there either.

A teacher named Miss Kim worked at the store. She saw Colton looking sad. "Small toys can roll," she said. "They roll far."

Near the carts, there was a big couch for sale. Colton got down on his knees. He peeked under the couch. Something blue was there! He reached his arm in. His fingers touched the little car. He pulled it out.

"My car!" said Colton. "It rolled under the couch!"

Mama helped him stand up. Miss Kim smiled and gave him a sticker with a star on it. Colton held the car with both hands now. He would draw a picture of the blue car when he got home.

"Mama, hold my hand too," said Colton. So she did.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Leo went to the park with Dad. Leo held Dad's hand. The sun felt hot on his head. His water bottle felt cold in his hand.

Leo saw the big slide. He wanted to go on it. He climbed the ladder with Dad right behind him. At the top, Leo lay down on his tummy. He put his head down first.

Dad said, "Not head first, Leo. At the playground, go down the slide feet first."

Leo sat up. He turned himself around. His feet went first. Whoosh! Down he went. His socks felt rough on the slide. He landed in the sand on his feet.

"Again!" said Leo. He climbed up again. Feet first. Whoosh! He kicked the sand at the bottom and laughed.

Then Leo saw a shiny can in the sand. He reached for it. Dad came fast and picked it up. "Not that one," said Dad. "It has sharp edges." Dad put it in the trash.

Leo stayed close to Dad. They sat on the bench. Dad opened the cold water bottle. Leo drank a little sip.

"More slide?" asked Dad.

"Feet first!" said Leo. He ran to the ladder.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Peyton sat on the rug at math club. Ten toy ducks sat in a row. Her teacher, Miss Kim, said, "Count them for me."

Peyton counted fast. "One, two, three... um..." She forgot where she stopped. "Ducks are tricky!"

Her friend Leo laughed. "They do not even wiggle!"

Peyton looked at her hands. She tried again. She held up one finger for each duck. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Miss Kim put out two plates of pretend cookies. "Which group has more?"

Peyton counted the cookies. She put up a finger for each one. "This plate has seven. That plate has four. Seven is more!"

"You may pick one cookie," said Miss Kim with a smile.

Peyton picked the sweet pink one. "Mmm, counting makes cookies fair!"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Amira wanted to make cookies for her family. She stood at the little table in the cooking classroom. The teacher put out a big bag of sugar. Amira picked up the bag. She tipped it over the bowl. The sugar poured out fast. Too much sugar fell in. Sugar went all over the table.

The teacher brought a small cup. "This is a measuring cup," she said. Amira looked at it. It had a little line inside. Amira filled the cup with sugar. She stopped at the line. Then she poured it into the bowl. Not too much, not too little. Just the right amount.

Amira measured the flour too. She measured a little spoon of vanilla. The teacher put the tray in the hot oven. Amira waited and watched from far away. Soon the cookies were done. She put them in her sheep lunchbox to carry home. "My family will know I made these," said Amira. Her dad took a big bite. "These are so nice," he said.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Baby Ben was sleeping in his crib. Brielle stood on her tiptoes. She wanted Ben to like her.

"Can I hold his hand?" she asked.

"Shh, soft hands," said Mom. "You can put one finger in his hand."

Brielle counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." She picked her pointer finger. She put it in Ben's little hand.

Ben held tight! His small fingers gripped her finger.

"He got me!" said Brielle. She giggled.

She pulled a tiny bit. Ben still held on. He was so strong for a baby.

"You are so cute," she whispered.

Ben opened his eyes. Sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the crib.

Brielle waited. She waited some more. Then Ben blinked at her.

"Hi, Ben," she said.

Mom clapped her hands, very softly. "He likes you," she said.

Brielle counted again. "One finger, one baby, one big sister."

Ben squeezed her finger one more time.

"Again tomorrow?" Brielle asked.

story:
Bennett ran into the backyard. "Can I get in the tub now?" he asked. A big tub of water sat by the fence. It was tall, and it sparkled in the light.

"I want to jump in!" said Bennett. He lifted one foot.

"Not yet," said Grandma. She put her hand in the water. "The sun made it too hot. We will add cold water and mix it." Bennett watched. Grandma turned the hose on. The water went round and round.

"Now let me check," said Grandma. She put her hand in again. "It is warm now. Not hot. You can get in."

Bennett put in his toes. "It feels nice!" He splashed with both hands. "You do the checking every time?" he asked.

"Every time," said Grandma. She smiled and held his hand so he would not slip.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Sebastian went to the library with his mom. The craft table had smooth white paper and cups of paint. The librarian smiled. "You can paint one half of the paper," she said. "Then fold it while the paint is wet."

Sebastian dug his brush into the red paint. He painted one wing on one half of the paper. One wing, one dot, one line. Then he folded the paper in half. He pressed it with his hands.

"Open it," said the librarian. Sebastian opened the paper slowly. Two wings! Both sides matched. "A butterfly," Sebastian said. The wet paint had made a print on the other half.

"Mine has one wing only," said a girl next to him. She had let her paint dry. "Try again," said Sebastian. "Fold it while it is wet." She painted blue on one half. She folded it fast. She opened it. Two blue wings, the same on each side.

Sebastian carried his butterfly to the kitchen window at home. He hung it up with tape. "One butterfly," he said. "Two wings. Both the same." His mom clapped her hands.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jules sat at the dinner table. His tooth felt wiggly. He wiggled it with his tongue.

Dad put down his fork. Dad did not eat. Dad made a big sigh.

"What is wrong?" asked Jules.

"I feel nervous," said Dad. "Tomorrow I go to my new job. My tummy feels funny."

Jules felt surprised. He thought only kids got scared. Grown-ups were so big!

"You get scared too?" asked Jules.

"Yes," said Dad. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Jules felt happy inside. He ran to get his teddy. He put teddy near Dad's plate.

"Teddy helps me when I'm scared," said Jules.

Dad hugged teddy. Then Dad smiled a big smile. Dad took a big bite of dinner.

"Teddy works," said Dad. "Teddy works!"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Noah stood at the train station. He held a red paper sign. It said "Grandma" in wobbly letters. He had drawn it all by himself. One letter looked a bit wrong. But Mom said it was still good.

The train came in. It was very long and loud. People stepped down, one by one. Then Noah saw her. "Grandma!" he shouted. She waved and hugged him tight. "I get to stay for a whole week," she said.

At home, Noah showed Grandma his toy train. "Dad has a train too," said Noah. Grandma laughed. "When your dad was little, he had a blue bike. He fell off it lots of times. Then one day he rode it all the way to the shop." Noah stared. "Dad was little? Like me?" "Yes," said Grandma. "Just like you."

The next day, Noah rode his trike in the yard. He fell off. His mouth turned down. "That's okay," said Grandma. "Your dad fell too." Noah got back on. He pushed and pushed. Then the trike rolled fast down the little hill. "I did it!" said Noah. "Tell me another dad story tonight!" Grandma smiled. "I will," she said.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Sadie stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her new lunchbox with a little boat on it. She liked the blue sails best.

At lunch time, Sadie could not find her lunchbox. Another girl had one just like it. The same boat. The same blue sails. The other girl looked sad too. "That one is mine," Sadie said softly. "But this one is mine," said the girl.

Then Sadie's teacher came. She opened the lid. Inside, there was a name. It said Sadie. "This one is Sadie's," said the teacher. The other girl opened the other box. That lid had her own name. It said Mia. Now they each had the right lunch.

After lunch, Sadie asked the teacher for a marker. She wrote Sadie on her coat tag too. She wrote it on her backpack. At home that night, Sadie helped Mom stir the soup for dinner. Then she found her old teddy. "We will write your name too," she said. She printed the letters, one by one. "There. Now you can always come back to me."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Levi ran to the big paint table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. A big, round, orange pumpkin. But he looked and looked. There was no orange paint.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Levi, counting the pots. "Red, yellow, blue." No orange anywhere. He frowned at the empty paint cups. His pumpkin could not be a green pumpkin. Or a blue one. Pumpkins were orange.

Levi dipped his brush in the red pot. He made a thin red circle. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow pot. He swirled the yellow right on top. The red circle turned orange! "Orange!" shouted Levi. He painted the whole pumpkin orange. It looked like a giant sunset egg, glowing on the paper.

He held it up high. "I made orange!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Everett ran to the big tree at the playground. The sky was cloudy and soft. Under the tree was a pretend kitchen. There were cups and pots and one long stick for a spoon. "I will cook soup," said Everett. He took all the pots. He took all the cups too.

Then Mia came to the tree. She stood very still. She had no pot. She had no cup. Her hands were empty. "I want to cook too," said Mia. Everett looked at his pots. He looked at Mia's empty hands.

"You can use this pot," said Everett. He put a pot in her hands. He put a cup in her hands too. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too," said Mia. She smiled big. Now they both had pots. Now they both could cook.

"Stir, stir, stir," said Everett. "Stir, stir, stir," said Mia. They stirred the leaf soup under the cloudy sky. Ben ran over. He had no pot. Everett looked at his last pot. "You can use it too," said Everett. Ben stirred and stirred. Three friends cooked soup by the big tree. "More leaves for the soup!" said Ben.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Wyatt wanted warm milk. He followed Dad into the kitchen. Dad turned a knob on the stove. The pot went on the little burner. Wyatt could not see anything. The burner did not look hot at all. Wyatt reached out his hand. Dad caught it gently. "Only grown-ups touch the stove," Dad said. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot." Wyatt stepped back. He sat on his stool and watched. The milk got warm. Bubbles came up, small and slow. Dad poured the milk into Wyatt's cup. It was warm, not cold like before.

Wyatt carried his cup outside. He stayed close to Dad in the backyard. The grass was wet under his shoes. A bee buzzed by the big flowers. Wyatt did not touch the bee. He watched it fly away. Dad picked up a sharp tool from the ground. Dad put it far back on the shelf. Wyatt sipped his milk. "I like the warm taste," he said. The sun came out. The wet grass began to shine. Dad held out his hand. Wyatt took it and held on tight. "One more sip," said Wyatt, "and then can we look for birds?"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Margot sat at the dinner table. She had five toy monkeys with her. They sat next to her cup. "Time to sing," said Margot.

She sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Then one monkey fell off. Margot put it in her lap. "How many now?" she asked. She counted, "One, two, three, four." Four monkeys sat by the cup. She sang again. One more monkey fell off. Now three. Then two. Then one. The last monkey fell off, and her lap was full.

Daddy slid her plate closer. "Little monkeys need dinner too," he said. Margot lined up the monkeys. She pointed at each one. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. All five monkeys sat back up again. "Maybe they should not jump on the bed," said Margot. Then she took a big bite of her peas.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Matthew went to the farmers' market with Dad. There were big baskets of carrots and potatoes. "Let's buy some," said Dad. "You can help cook supper." Matthew picked three carrots. They felt bumpy in his hand. A fish seller next door waved. "Look at the shiny fish!" said Matthew. "Yes, very shiny," said Dad.

At home, Dad put the carrots on the counter. Matthew looked closely. The carrots had dirt on them. Brown dirt, right on the top. "Dirt," said Matthew. "I don't want dirt in my soup." He felt worried. "We can fix that," said Dad. He lifted Matthew up to the sink.

Matthew turned the water on. The water ran cool over the carrots. He rubbed them with his hands. The dirt came off. It went down the drain. "Look, Dad! The dirt goes away!" Dad smiled. "Good scrubbing," he said. Then they rinsed the potatoes too. Scrub, rinse, clean. Scrub, rinse, clean. Soon every carrot was orange and shiny.

Dad chopped the carrots with a big knife. Matthew stood back, far from the knife. He watched Dad put the pot on the stove. "You can stir when it cools," said Dad. The soup bubbled and smelled good. Mom came home and sniffed the air. "Mmm! Who made this?" she asked.

"I did!" said Matthew. "I scrubbed the dirt off!" They all sat down together. Matthew ate his soup. The carrots were soft and sweet. "Clean carrots, yummy soup," said Matthew. Dad gave him a high five. "Scrub, rinse, clean," said Matthew, and he took one more bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James was at Grandma's house. He put on his red coat all by himself. One arm went in. Then the other arm went in. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It stuck near the top. He tugged it gently. Zip! It closed.

"Good job," said Grandma. "Now we can play outside." James ran in the snow. His hands got cold. He had lost one mitten by the big tree. He looked and looked. There it was, under the bench.

Grandma held his mittens. "Try your coat pocket," she said. James pushed both mittens in. The pocket held them snug. They stayed put.

Later they went inside. James was thirsty, so Grandma gave him milk. They ate a cheese sandwich together.

"Thank you, Grandma," said James. He patted his pocket. The mittens were still right there.
